prompt: Your school is considering a student-led peer support programme for mental health and wellbeing. Write a text for school leaders in which you explain potential benefits and risks, recommend safeguards and training, and clarify what peer supporters should and should not be expected to do.
requirements: Explain potential benefits and risks of peer support.
Clarify the limits of peer supporters' responsibilities.
purpose: Recommend a safe, limited peer support programme
textTypeRationale: A proposal allows the writer to define purpose, safeguards, training and limits for a school decision.
modelAnswerJa: Peer supportをprofessional counsellingの代替にしないことを明確にし、benefitとriskの両方を扱っています。Safeguards・training・boundariesを分けたproposal構成です。
modelAnswer:
Proposal: A Safe Peer Support Programme for Student Wellbeing

Purpose

This proposal recommends a student-led peer support programme that provides an accessible first point of contact for students while maintaining clear boundaries between peer support and professional mental-health care.

Potential benefits

Students do not always approach adults first when they are struggling. Speaking to a trained peer can feel less formal and may help someone describe a problem before it becomes more serious. Peer supporters could also reduce isolation by listening without judgment and directing students toward existing school services.

A visible programme could improve school culture more broadly. Training a group of students in active listening, confidentiality and referral procedures would create more informed conversations about wellbeing and reduce the idea that asking for help is embarrassing.

Risks

The main risk is expecting students to handle problems beyond their competence. Peer supporters are not therapists. They should never be responsible for diagnosing conditions, providing treatment, investigating abuse or keeping dangerous information secret.

Confidentiality also needs careful limits. Students may assume that private means nothing can ever be shared. The programme must explain from the beginning that concerns involving immediate safety, self-harm, abuse or serious risk must be passed to a designated adult.

Training

Selected peer supporters should complete structured training led by qualified school staff or external professionals. Training should cover active listening, respectful language, cultural sensitivity, boundaries, referral procedures and what to do when a conversation becomes overwhelming.

Role

Peer supporters should be expected to listen, help students identify next steps and connect them with appropriate adults or services. They should not offer medical advice, promise secrecy, meet students alone off campus or become available at all hours.

The school should provide regular supervision. A staff coordinator could hold short weekly check-ins where peer supporters can discuss general challenges without revealing unnecessary personal details. Supporters should also be able to step back temporarily if the role affects their own wellbeing.

Access and privacy

The programme should have clear contact methods, such as scheduled lunchtime sessions or a referral form, rather than informal messaging through personal social-media accounts. Records should be minimal and handled by staff, not students.

Review

A one-term pilot would allow the school to evaluate participation, referral patterns and anonymous feedback. The review should ask whether students understand the limits of the service and whether peer supporters feel adequately trained and supported.

Conclusion

Peer support can be valuable precisely because students are not professionals: they can offer human connection in a familiar environment. But that strength becomes a danger if the school treats them as substitute counsellors. A successful programme must therefore be built around training, supervision, referral and clear limits.

With those safeguards, peer support could make it easier for students to take the first step toward help without placing an unfair responsibility on the students providing it.

prompt: A local newspaper is debating whether public transport fares for teenagers should be reduced. Write a text in response in which you explain possible social and environmental benefits, address concerns about cost and fairness, and argue for a practical policy.
requirements: Explain social and environmental benefits of lower youth fares.
Address concerns about cost and fairness.
Argue for a realistic policy rather than a simple free-transport demand.
purpose: Argue for an affordable youth-fare policy
textTypeRationale: A letter to the editor directly enters a local public debate and can respond to common objections.
modelAnswerJa: 無料化を単純に要求せず、targeted discountと評価方法を提案しています。Costとfairnessへの反論を扱うことでpublic argumentを深めています。
modelAnswer:
Dear Editor,

Your recent article on rising public transport costs asked whether teenagers should receive larger fare reductions. I believe the answer is yes, but the strongest case is not that young people simply deserve cheaper travel. A well-designed youth fare can improve access to education, reduce car dependence and help families manage essential costs.

For many teenagers, transport is not optional. Students travel to school, part-time jobs, sports, libraries and medical appointments. When fares rise, families with several children feel the increase immediately. Young people in lower-income households may begin refusing activities because the journey costs too much. Equal access to education means little if some students cannot afford to reach opportunities outside the classroom.

Lower fares can also create long-term environmental benefits. Travel habits develop early. If teenagers learn that buses and trains are convenient and affordable, they are more likely to continue using them as adults. A city that wants to reduce congestion and emissions should make public transport a realistic first choice before young people become dependent on cars.

Critics reasonably ask who will pay. Transport systems need drivers, maintenance, energy and reliable service. Making every journey free without additional funding could reduce revenue and eventually damage service quality. That would help nobody.

For this reason, I support a targeted discount rather than unlimited free travel. Residents aged 13 to 18 could receive a substantial reduction using an existing transport card. The discount could apply all day so that students with after-school activities are not penalized. The city should compensate transport operators from its mobility or climate budget instead of expecting them to absorb the full cost.

There is also a fairness question. Why should teenagers receive support when adults on low incomes also struggle with fares? The answer should not be to remove youth discounts; it should be to design transport policy around need. Reduced fares for students can exist alongside income-based support for adults, older residents and disabled passengers.

The policy should be tested rather than defended by slogans. After one year, the city could compare youth ridership, total revenue, car journeys near schools and participation in after-school programmes. If the discount increases use without creating an unsustainable funding gap, it should continue. If not, the structure can be adjusted.

Affordable transport is social infrastructure. It connects people to education, work and community life. Teenagers are at a stage when independence is growing but income is limited. A practical youth discount would recognize that reality while also supporting the city’s environmental goals.

Cheaper fares alone will not fix an unreliable bus system, but price is one barrier the city can remove. It should do so carefully, measure the results and then improve the policy with evidence.

Yours faithfully,

A local resident

prompt: Your school is preparing an information campaign for students who have part-time jobs. Write a text in which you explain common workplace rights and responsibilities, identify situations in which students should seek help, and give practical advice for balancing work and school.
requirements: Explain common rights and responsibilities of young workers.
Identify situations in which students should seek help.
Give practical advice for balancing employment and school.
audience: Students with or considering part-time jobs
purpose: Provide clear, practical guidance for young workers
textTypeRationale: A brochure is well suited to practical information because it can use clear headings, short sections and direct advice.
modelAnswerJa: Brochureとしてheadingsと短いsectionsを使い、rightsだけでなくresponsibilitiesとschool balanceも含めています。読者がすぐ行動できるpractical adviceを優先しています。
modelAnswer:
Your First Part-Time Job: Know Your Rights, Do Your Part

Starting a part-time job can give you money, confidence and useful experience. It can also be the first time you have to understand workplace rules for yourself. Knowing your rights does not mean expecting special treatment. It means understanding what a fair workplace looks like and what responsibilities you have in return.

Know the basics

Employment rules differ by country and age, so check official local guidance. In general, young workers should receive clear information about pay, hours and duties. You should know when you are expected to work, how much you will be paid and who to contact if you cannot attend.

Keep copies of schedules, contracts and payslips. If something seems wrong later, accurate records are more useful than trying to remember a conversation from several weeks ago.

Safety comes first

You have a responsibility to follow safety instructions, use equipment correctly and ask questions when you do not understand a task. Employers also have a responsibility to provide a safe environment and appropriate training.

Do not pretend you understand a dangerous task because you are embarrassed to ask. If you are told to use unfamiliar equipment, handle unsafe materials or work in a situation that feels genuinely dangerous, stop and seek advice from a supervisor or trusted adult.

Respect works both ways

Arrive on time, communicate clearly and treat colleagues and customers respectfully. If you make a mistake, admit it and learn from it. Being a young worker does not remove ordinary workplace responsibilities.

At the same time, being inexperienced does not make bullying, discrimination or harassment acceptable. Repeated humiliating comments, unwanted sexual behaviour, threats or unfair treatment based on identity should not be dismissed as just part of having a job.

When should you seek help?

Talk to a trusted adult, manager, union, school adviser or appropriate official service if:
• you are not being paid what was agreed;
• you are repeatedly asked to work hours that may be illegal for your age;
• you face harassment or discrimination;
• you are pressured to do unsafe work;
• you are threatened for raising a reasonable concern.

If you are unsure, asking for information is a sensible first step. You do not need to wait until a situation becomes serious.

Protect your school time

A part-time job should add experience, not remove your ability to study or sleep. Be realistic about how many hours you can manage. During examination periods, speak to your employer early if you need reduced availability.

Use a calendar for shifts, deadlines and major assessments. Avoid accepting extra hours automatically because saying yes feels easier in the moment.

Build skills, not just a paycheque

Notice what you are learning: communication, teamwork, problem-solving, customer service and time management. These skills can be valuable long after the job ends.

A good first job should teach you how to contribute responsibly while expecting fair treatment in return. Know the rules, ask questions and remember that being young does not mean your safety or dignity matters less.
